FaRMING aS a JOB: THE FULL PICTURE

July 8, 2026July 15, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:01
Instaread

Farming isn’t all overalls and neatly arranging processed produce at a market booth; while that’s part of the picture, there’s a lot that goes into the life of a small-scale farmer. So, what does that look like day-to-day? We asked. 

When asked about how much time is spent actually growing food, Chris Swinson of Grand Rapids’ Mycophile’s Garden estimates that he spends about a third of his workweek in cultivation. Dan Owens of Bankson Lake Farm in Lawton brings that estimate down to 5-10%. He explains that once plants are in the ground, a majority of hands-in-the-dirt farming is ‘watering, weeding and waiting’.

So what does a farmer spend their day doing? First of all, cleaning. At Bankson Lake, the cleaning list spans from harvesting lugs to washing and bubbling the greens themselves. And for mushroom-focused Mycophile’s Garden, it takes a close-to-sterile environment to produce their large range of fungi. 

Once the product is harvested, it then needs to be packaged and delivered to grocery stores and restaurants, a process that takes up another third of Swinson’s workweek. Driving a distribution route was something that Owens originally pictured delegating to another team member, but quickly found that a personal connection to the farmer was important for customers – so he often personally delivers products once a week. 

For direct consumers, both businesses attend local farmers markets. For farmers, this is a process that includes harvesting, packaging, and packing before driving to the market itself, where they’ll need to set up tents, signs, and displays. When the market ends, the entire process happens in reverse – pack up, head back, and put everything back in cold storage. It’s a full day’s work! 

For this reason, Swinson expresses gratitude for a dependable team. After eleven years of business, most of their market staff have been with them for 5 years, which says a lot for a job that can start at 5 am. 

Beyond markets and delivery routes, weeding, or putting rubber bands around bunches of carrots, a farmer can be found doing all sorts of ordering and other office tasks, or even just being there for when a problem arises. For example, Owens explained that he had irrigation to fix right after our conversation. He also notes that “many small-scale farmers have to have an off-farm job in addition to working full time or more growing and selling veggies, fruits, mushrooms, herbs, flowers and more.”

With all these tasks at hand, both business owners still focus on creating a work-life balance. For Swinson, that’s made possible by growth and working with a team. For Owens, that means focusing on accessible goals and knowing when a day’s work is done. For a job that can mean no weekends, keeping balance is an important task as well. 

The next time you pick up an onion or a box of specialty coral tooth mushrooms, savor them a bit more, knowing the full picture of what went into getting them on your plate.
